questions.title: Muscle preventing pelvic tilt on one-leg stance
questions.question: Which muscle prevents pelvic tilt to the unsupported side when standing on one leg?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gluteus maximus is the powerful hip extensor used in climbing and rising from sitting, but it plays only a minor role in stabilising the pelvis during single-leg stance. It is not the muscle this question is testing.
explanations.B: Correct. Gluteus medius (with gluteus minimus), supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, contracts on the stance-leg side during single-leg support and pulls the pelvis down on that side, which keeps the unsupported side from dropping. This is the exact mechanism disrupted in a Trendelenburg (waddling) gait when the superior gluteal nerve or these abductors fail. It is the muscle group specifically responsible for pelvic stabilisation during walking and single-leg stance. This is a common "which muscle is missing" exam pattern, so recognising gluteus medius specifically (rather than the more familiar gluteus maximus) is the point being tested.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Obturator externus is a small lateral rotator of the hip, supplied by the obturator nerve, and takes no part in frontal-plane pelvic stabilisation during stance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Obturator internus is also a lateral rotator of the extended hip (and an abductor when the hip is flexed), not a pelvic stabiliser during single-leg standing.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Quadratus femoris is a short lateral rotator of the hip near the intertrochanteric crest; like the other short rotators it does not stabilise the pelvis in the coronal plane during gait.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gluteus medius as the muscle that prevents pelvic drop to the unsupported side during single-leg stance.

questions.title: Movement lost completely in femoral nerve paralysis
questions.question: After complete paralysis of the femoral nerve, which of the following movements is lost completely?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hip flexion is produced mainly by iliopsoas (partly femoral-nerve-supplied via sartorius/pectineus, but psoas major is innervated directly by lumbar plexus roots) and by other flexors such as sartorius; it is weakened, not completely lost, since several non-femoral contributors remain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Thigh adduction is the job of the adductor group, supplied by the obturator nerve, which is untouched by a femoral nerve lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lateral rotation of the thigh is produced chiefly by the short rotators and gluteal muscles (obturator and sciatic-nerve-related territory), not by femoral-nerve-supplied muscles.
explanations.D: Correct. Quadriceps femoris is the only knee extensor in the body, and it is supplied entirely by the femoral nerve; no other muscle can substitute for it. A complete femoral nerve palsy therefore abolishes knee extension completely, unlike hip flexion, which several non-femoral muscles can still partly produce. This is why an isolated femoral nerve palsy is tested by asking a patient to actively extend the knee against resistance rather than by testing hip flexion alone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Knee flexion is produced by the hamstrings (tibial nerve) and other posterior thigh and leg muscles, none of which are femoral-nerve-supplied.

questions.learning_objective: Identify complete loss of knee extension as the deficit that follows total femoral nerve paralysis, since quadriceps femoris is its only muscle with no alternative nerve supply.

questions.title: Muscle supplied by the tibial nerve
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is supplied by the tibial nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Obturator internus is supplied by the nerve to obturator internus (a branch of the sacral plexus), not the tibial nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior lies in the anterior compartment of the leg and is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve, the opposite compartment's nerve to the tibial nerve's posterior-compartment territory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peroneus longus lies in the lateral compartment and is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve, again not the tibial nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gracilis is a hip adductor supplied by the obturator nerve, unrelated to the tibial nerve's leg territory.
explanations.E: Correct. Tibialis posterior lies in the deep posterior compartment of the leg, and like the rest of that compartment (gastrocnemius, soleus, the long toe flexors) it is supplied by the tibial nerve, the sciatic nerve's medial terminal division. This deep-compartment placement, alongside the tibial nerve's other targets (gastrocnemius, soleus, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus), is a frequently tested contrast with the anterior and lateral compartments' separate nerve supplies.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tibialis posterior as a posterior-compartment muscle supplied by the tibial nerve.

questions.title: Muscle that unlocks the knee joint
questions.question: Which muscle performs its function in the unlocking of knee joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plantaris is a vestigial muscle with a long thin tendon that assists weakly in plantar flexion; it has no role in unlocking the knee.
explanations.B: Correct. Popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the fixed tibia (in weight-bearing), reversing the screw-home mechanism that locks the fully extended knee, which is exactly what lets flexion begin. This is a classic "which muscle is different" pairing question, since popliteus's rotational action is easy to confuse with a simple flexor action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Soleus is a posterior-leg plantar flexor of the ankle that does not cross the knee joint at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrocnemius does cross the knee and assists weak flexion, but the specific unlocking action belongs to popliteus, whose rotation initiates the release of the screw-home lock.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Biceps femoris is a hamstring that flexes the knee once it is already unlocked, but it is not the muscle credited with the unlocking rotation itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify popliteus as the muscle that unlocks the fully extended knee, reversing the screw-home mechanism.

questions.title: Muscle that everts the foot at the subtalar joint
questions.question: Which one of the following muscles causes eversion of the foot at the subtalar joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum longus is primarily a toe extensor and weak ankle dorsiflexor; it contributes little to subtalar eversion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot, the opposite action to eversion.
explanations.C: Correct. Peroneus (fibularis) longus, together with peroneus brevis, everts the foot at the subtalar joint; its tendon also crosses the sole to help support the transverse arch. This eversion action is the standard contrast drawn against tibialis anterior and posterior, both of which invert rather than evert the foot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrocnemius is a plantar flexor of the ankle acting mainly in the sagittal plane, not an evertor.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Extensor hallucis longus extends the great toe and assists dorsiflexion, not eversion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify peroneus longus as the muscle that everts the foot at the subtalar joint.

questions.title: Muscles innervated by the axillary nerve
questions.question: Which muscles are innervated by the axillary nerve?

options.C: Pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscle
options.D: Latissimus dorsi and teres major muscles

explanations.A: Incorrect. Supraspinatus and infraspinatus are both supplied by the suprascapular nerve, not the axillary nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Infraspinatus is suprascapular-nerve territory, and teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve; neither is axillary-nerve territory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pectoralis major and pectoralis minor are supplied by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves, unrelated to the axillary nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve and teres major by the lower subscapular nerve; neither is axillary.
explanations.E: Correct. The axillary nerve, a terminal branch of the posterior cord, winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies deltoid (the main shoulder abductor) and teres minor (a lateral rotator and one of the SITS rotator cuff muscles), which is why a shoulder dislocation or humeral neck fracture that damages this nerve weakens both. This dual-muscle loss (deltoid for abduction, teres minor for lateral rotation) is exactly what follows a shoulder dislocation or surgical-neck-of-humerus fracture that damages the nerve at the quadrangular space.

questions.learning_objective: Identify deltoid and teres minor as the two muscles supplied by the axillary nerve.

questions.title: Branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus
questions.question: Which one of the following nerve is a branch of the lateral cord of the branchial plexus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The upper subscapular nerve is a posterior cord branch, not a lateral cord branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The long thoracic nerve arises directly from the roots (C5-C7), before any cord has formed, so it belongs to neither the lateral nor the posterior cord.
explanations.C: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve is one of the lateral cord's two terminal branches (with the lateral root of the median nerve); it pierces coracobrachialis and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. Its origin from the lateral cord, rather than directly from the roots or from a different cord, is the specific fact this style of question repeatedly tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk, well before the cords form, not from the lateral cord.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The thoracodorsal nerve is a posterior cord branch, supplying latissimus dorsi, not a lateral cord branch.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the musculocutaneous nerve as a terminal branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus.

questions.title: Muscle supplied by the common peroneal part of the sciatic nerve
questions.question: The following muscle is supplied by common peroneal part of sciatic nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The long head of biceps femoris arises from the ischial tuberosity, like the other hamstrings, and is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
explanations.B: Correct. The short head of biceps femoris is the developmental exception among the hamstrings: it arises from the linea aspera of the femur (not the ischial tuberosity), acts only at the knee, and is supplied by the common peroneal (fibular) division of the sciatic nerve rather than the tibial division. This selective sparing is the clinical basis for the observation that some knee flexion can persist even when a proximal sciatic injury has damaged the tibial division.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Semitendinosus is a true hamstring from the ischial tuberosity, supplied by the tibial division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Semimembranosus is likewise a true hamstring from the ischial tuberosity, tibial-division-supplied.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ischial (hamstring) part of adductor magnus is grouped functionally with the hamstrings and is tibial-division-supplied, unlike the short head of biceps femoris.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the short head of biceps femoris as the one hamstring supplied by the common peroneal, not tibial, division of the sciatic nerve.

questions.title: Gluteal injection site to avoid sciatic nerve injury
questions.question: To avoid sciatic nerve injury, an intramuscular injection in the gluteal region is given in which of the following quadrants?

options.E: Any one of the above quadrant

explanations.A: Correct. The sciatic nerve runs in the gluteal region roughly midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter, in the lower and medial part of the buttock; the upper outer quadrant sits well clear of this line, which is why intramuscular gluteal injections are placed there. This is the anatomical basis for the standard nursing and clinical teaching to always inject in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower outer quadrant is closer to the sciatic nerve's course than the upper outer quadrant, and is not the standard safe site.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The upper inner quadrant is closer to major neurovascular structures medially and is not the conventional injection site.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lower inner quadrant lies directly over the sciatic nerve's expected course and is the most dangerous quadrant to inject.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The quadrants are not interchangeable; only the upper outer quadrant reliably avoids the sciatic nerve.

questions.learning_objective: State that the upper outer quadrant of the buttock is the safe site for intramuscular gluteal injection, avoiding the sciatic nerve.

questions.title: Nerve damaged in buttock knife wound causing waddling gait
questions.question: Patient with a deep knife wound in the buttock walks with a waddling gait that is characterized by the pelvis falling toward one side at each step. Which of the following nerves is damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Obturator nerve injury weakens hip adduction and produces medial thigh sensory loss, not a waddling gait.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nerve to obturator internus supplies a small lateral rotator; its loss does not produce a Trendelenburg gait.
explanations.C: Correct. The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, which stabilise the pelvis during single-leg stance; its injury produces exactly this waddling (Trendelenburg) gait, with the pelvis dropping toward the unsupported side with each step on the injured side. This Trendelenburg-type gait is a classic bedside clue pointing directly to superior gluteal nerve damage rather than to a more proximal sciatic or lumbosacral plexus lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inferior gluteal nerve injury weakens gluteus maximus (hip extension, rising from sitting) but does not produce this pelvis-drop gait pattern.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Femoral nerve injury weakens knee extension and hip flexion, producing a different gait disturbance (buckling knee), not a waddling gait.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a Trendelenburg (waddling) gait as the sign of superior gluteal nerve injury and loss of gluteus medius/minimus pelvic stabilisation.
